candidates.title: The global memory shortage hits the MacBook Air
candidates.description: The global memory chip shortage appears to be affecting the availability of Apple’s most popular Mac.
candidates.body_text: In Brief Posted: The global memory chip shortage is affecting the availability of Apple’s most popular Mac, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman . Gurman said the shortage — caused by the demands of chip-hungry AI companies — had already affected Apple’s more niche computers, the Mac mini and Mac Studio. But it seems the company is now struggling to keep the MacBook Air in stock, with retailers saying that supply seems to be more constrained than ever before. Indeed, anyone trying to buy a MacBook Air from the Apple website will have to wait until the back half of August — or for certain configurations, until September. Gurman says Apple is working to address the issue by raising prices and sourcing memory from Chinese suppliers. Meanwhile, the company delayed its latest back-to-school promotion from June. And for the first time, the marketing material is more focused on the base model of the MacBook Pro. It even warns , “MacBook Air subject to availability.” Topics Scale faster. Grow your portfolio. candidates.body_text: PC Components CPUs AMD's upcoming Zen 6 processors could fix microstutters and improve 1% lows in games — Next-gen CPUs tipped to feature per-core optimizations for thermal and power budgets News By Hassam Nasir Published 11 hours ago It's the small things that matter. (Image credit: AMD) Share this article 17 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter AMD is expected to unveil its next-gen Zen 6 platform at CES 2026 with Ryzen 10000 series processors. While we're looking forward to IPC and clock speed improvements, it seems like more subtle, under-the-hood changes could end up upgrading the gaming experience in a big way. According to a tip received by Videocardz, AMD is implementing various per-core optimizations to ensure foreground tasks get priority over background applications. Each new feature is supposed to more smartly manage the power and thermal budgets at the silicon's disposal, so let's go over each of them. First up, we have CPPC Performance Priority — CPPC stands for Collaborative Processor Performance Control, and it's responsible for communication between the silicon and the OS. It lets the firmware sitting in between decide the performance of each core separately. This feature has actually existed since the Ryzen 3000 series, but it doesn't work perfectly. candidates.title: My late grandparents are frozen in time on Google Maps - it's my favourite place on the internet
candidates.description: My late grandparents are frozen in time on Google Maps - it's my favourite place on the internet    BBC
candidates.body_text: My late grandparents are frozen in time on Google Maps - it's my favourite place on the internet 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Leigh Boobyer BBC Wales Chelsea Boyce Chelsea Boyce's video on Instagram shows her grandparents in the door of their Cardiff home in 2011 before they died A woman whose grandparents are "frozen in time" on Google Street View has called it "forever my favourite place on the internet". Ted Boyce and Beryl Boyce can be seen on Google as he holds open the door for her at their home on Cardiff Road in Creigiau, a village just outside of Cardiff. Chelsea Boyce, 31, from London, said the picture was captured in 2011, the year her granddad died, and it "warms my heart every time I see it and it just brings back a lot of memories". Posting a video of her visiting the house on Instagram, she received many sweet messages from people who said they also used Google Maps to see their late loved ones. The model and photoshoot producer said her grandparents were born and raised in Wales and she spent most childhood holidays visiting their home. Ted, who was a musical director for BBC Wales, died in 2011 followed by Beryl six years later. candidates.title: Apple struggles to keep pace with AI ‘bug’ hunters
candidates.description: Apple struggles to keep pace with AI ‘bug’ hunters    Financial Times
candidates.body_text: © Bloomberg Apple struggles to keep pace with AI ‘bug’ hunters on x (opens in a new window) Apple struggles to keep pace with AI ‘bug’ hunters on facebook (opens in a new window) Apple struggles to keep pace with AI ‘bug’ hunters on linkedin (opens in a new window) Save current progress 0% Tom Wilson in London and Michael Acton in San Francisco PublishedYESTERDAY 85 Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Apple has restricted the number of potentially dangerous software bugs researchers can submit to its internal security team, as it faces a deluge of reports from people using AI models to identify alleged risks. The Cupertino-based tech giant told the FT it had moved in June to limit the high volume of requests it was receiving, with its review system coming under pressure from “AI slop” reports that can hallucinate security risks in its software. Apple is grappling with an industry-wide phenomenon that has resulted in generative AI software tools transforming the cyber security arms race, with an increase in the detection of real security flaws and a wave of poor-quality submissions from amateur bug hunters using AI, the company said. The change in Apple’s approach was highlighted by Italian cyber security start-up Bynario, which told the FT it had used OpenAI’s ChatGPT to identify more than 50 bugs in the latest version of the MacBook operating system in just three weeks.
